title: Conflicts: What They Are, How They Resolve

questions.prompt: A rebase stops on a conflict. You want the version that was on your branch before the rebase started. Which command gets it?
options: git checkout --ours <file>, because those changes were yours
git checkout --theirs <file>, because during a rebase you are the incoming side
git checkout --ours <file>, followed by git rebase --skip
Neither works — during a rebase both sides come from your branch
questions.explanation: During a rebase, HEAD is the branch you are replaying onto, so the side labelled theirs is the one you brought with you. The temptation to reach for `--ours` is exactly the trap (A, and C with a skip that also discards work). Both sides are labelled in the file (D) — read the labels at the top of the conflict rather than relying on which words feel right.

questions.prompt: A merge left markers in three files and git printed a wall of output. What is the first command to run?
options: git status, then git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U to get the exact unresolved list
Open each conflicting file and start deleting markers
git checkout --theirs . to clear everything, then read the diff
git rebase --continue to skip past the conflict
questions.explanation: Get the list before reading files — the terminal output mixes conflicts with progress noise, and `--diff-filter=U` names exactly the paths git still considers unresolved. Deleting markers file by file (B) is what happens next, but starting from a list means you know when you are done. Bulk-taking theirs (C) silently discards your own work, and `--continue` (D) is for a rebase in progress and will not resolve anything here.

questions.prompt: Two branches both changed the same three lines of a config file, in different ways, and neither edit is obsolete. What is the correct resolution?
options: Take ours — the branch you are on is the one being reviewed
Take theirs — the incoming change is newer and therefore better
Combine both edits by hand into what the file should actually say, then git add it
Run git rebase and let git's merge algorithm decide
questions.explanation: When both edits are real, neither side is the answer — the question is what the file should say, and only you know that. Ours (A) and theirs (B) are preferences dressed as resolutions, and each silently deletes a real change. Rebase (D) applies the same merge machinery and will land on the same conflict; the algorithm was never going to decide this one.

questions.prompt: A merge conflicts over package-lock.json, which nobody edits by hand and which conflicts every few weeks. What is the actual fix?
options: Delete the file and regenerate it, committing the result
Configure a merge driver for it in .gitattributes so git resolves it without markers
Add it to .gitignore and stop tracking it
Always resolve it with --ours, since the lock file is machine-written
questions.explanation: The lesson's test is whether a human ever needs to decide anything about this file. For a generated lock file, the answer is no, so a configured merge driver in .gitattributes is the mechanism for that. Deleting it (A) and ignoring it (C) each trade a real problem for a worse one. Always taking ours (D) is not the same thing — it still produces a conflict every time and still needs a human to pick a side, which is precisely the cost you were trying to remove.
